questions.prompt: Duhaim, head of caseworkers, asks: "Did coaching raise employment for the seekers my caseworkers chose to coach last year?" Which summary answers him?
options: The average effect over every registered seeker
The effect on the seekers who were offered coaching
The value of the best rule under next year's budget
The difference in employment between coached and uncoached seekers
questions.explanation: He asks about the seekers who were offered coaching, so the estimand is the effect on the offered (ATT), not the average over everyone.
misconceptions: Answers for everyone, though he asked about the seekers his team chose
Answers a forward-looking decision, not a question about last year
Reads an observed difference as the effect, ignoring how caseworkers chose

questions.prompt: A vendor shows that Fursa's risk score predicts unemployment at six months with an AUC of 0.85 and proposes giving places to the top fifth by score. What is the main flaw?
options: An AUC of 0.85 is too low for a public decision
The score was trained on old data and may have drifted
The score ranks by need without coaching, not by what coaching changes
Places should be given at random to be fair
questions.explanation: The score predicts the outcome without coaching; the places should follow the difference coaching makes, which is a different quantity.
misconceptions: Treats the score's accuracy as the issue; a perfect score would have the same flaw
Names a real risk, but not the one that makes the ranking wrong
Confuses fairness of process with getting the most jobs from a budget

questions.prompt: In the logs, disabled seekers in Nijad were offered coaching in under 1% of decisions. A colleague still reports a doubly robust effect for them. What do you say?
options: The doubly robust estimator protects the estimate, so it can stand
The estimate for them rests on the outcome model's extrapolation; report it as such or not at all
Trim them out and report the trimmed effect as the effect for all seekers
Increase the number of folds so the group appears in every fold
questions.explanation: Without offered seekers like them, no weighting or matching can compare; only a model's extrapolation speaks for them.
misconceptions: Believes double robustness repairs a lack of overlap
Trims without saying that the estimand changed
Thinks a resampling choice can create data that were never collected

questions.prompt: Why does double machine learning use a score with residual corrections instead of averaging the difference of two outcome-model predictions?
options: The corrections make the estimate insensitive to small errors in the nuisance models
The corrections remove the need for a propensity model
The corrections make the estimate unbiased even with a hidden confounder
The corrections speed up the fitting of gradient boosting
questions.explanation: The orthogonal score has zero derivative in the nuisance models at the truth, so their regularisation errors enter only to second order.
misconceptions: Inverts the role of the corrections: they are built from the propensity model
Expects an estimator to fix information missing from the data
Mistakes a statistical property for a computational one

questions.prompt: On 40,000 logged decisions, regression adjustment with 60 controls gives 13.5 points (12.4 to 14.7) and DoubleML gives 10.8 (9.6 to 12.1). Without knowing the truth, which reasoning should guide the report?
options: Report the regression: its interval is narrower
Report the average of the two as a compromise
Report DoubleML: flexible nuisances and cross-fitting allow for nonlinear confounding that a linear model cannot follow
Report neither: the two disagree, so the data cannot answer
questions.explanation: The regression assumes linear confounding; DoubleML does not, and its interval is valid under weaker assumptions.
misconceptions: Treats a narrow interval as evidence of a correct model
Averages a biased and an unbiased estimator, keeping part of the bias
Takes disagreement between a restrictive and a flexible model as a sign that nothing is identified

questions.prompt: On the 2027 extract the DoubleML estimate is 12.8 points with a robustness value of 8.5%. What may you tell the director?
options: Coaching raised employment by 12.8 points, whatever is missing from the data
A hidden factor explaining under 8.5% of the remaining variation of both the offer and employment cannot erase the effect
There is an 8.5% chance that the effect is zero
The bias from the missing column is at most 8.5 points
questions.explanation: The robustness value is the confounder strength, on both partial R2 scales, that would bring the estimate to zero.
misconceptions: Reads a point estimate as robust to hidden confounding
Reads the robustness value as a probability
Confuses the strength of a confounder with the size of the bias

questions.prompt: Four nuisance learners give DML estimates from 11.0 to 14.2 points. How should the learner for the report be chosen?
options: By the lowest out-of-fold losses of the propensity and outcome models, fixed before seeing the estimates
By the estimate closest to what the caseworkers expect
By the smallest standard error
By the median of the four estimates
questions.explanation: Nuisance learners are judged by how well they predict, out of fold; choosing by the estimate invalidates the interval.
misconceptions: Lets the desired answer choose the method: a forking path
Treats precision as accuracy
Averages over learners known to be poor, keeping their bias

questions.prompt: In the X-learner on a 1:1 pilot, what is the imputed effect for a coached seeker who found work?
options: 1 minus the coached model's predicted chance for her
1 minus the uncoached model's predicted chance for her
The uncoached model's predicted chance minus 1
The difference between the two models' predictions for her
questions.explanation: For a coached seeker the missing outcome is the uncoached one, so the imputed effect is her observed outcome minus the uncoached model's prediction.
misconceptions: Uses her own arm's model, which predicts her observed outcome, not her missing one
Reverses the sign used for the coached arm
Describes the T-learner, not the imputation step

questions.prompt: A T-learner fitted with lightly regularised boosting on 1,800 seekers per arm predicts effects from minus 40 to plus 60 points. The true effects range from minus 10 to plus 30. What is the most likely cause?
options: Each arm's model fits its own noise, and the difference of two noisy predictions exaggerates heterogeneity
Confounding between the arms in the pilot
The outcome is binary, so effects cannot be estimated
The T-learner always shrinks effects towards zero
questions.explanation: Two separately fitted models subtract their errors; with weak regularisation the spread of predicted effects is mostly noise.
misconceptions: Blames confounding in a lottery
Treats a binary outcome as a barrier rather than a source of noise
Describes the S-learner's failure, the opposite of this one

questions.prompt: The causal forest ranks distance to the office as the second driver of effect variation. A manager proposes moving coaching closer to remote seekers to raise its effect. What do you say?
options: Agree: the forest shows distance causes smaller effects
Disagree: importance describes where effects differ, not what would happen if distance changed; a trial of the change would tell
Disagree: importance near the top is always an artefact of correlated features
Agree, if the forest's importance has a confidence interval above zero
questions.explanation: The effect of coaching is causal; how it varies with distance is a description, and moving the service is a different intervention.
misconceptions: Reads a moderator as a lever that can be changed
Overgeneralises a real caveat into a rule
Thinks statistical precision turns a description into a causal claim about a different intervention

questions.prompt: You want to check whether an effect model trained on the pilot's training split can be trusted. Which check is valid?
options: Compare its predictions with the observed outcomes of the training seekers
Sort the held-out randomised seekers into groups by prediction and compare each group's coached-minus-uncoached difference with its mean prediction
Compute the correlation between its predictions and the risk score
Report its R-squared on the held-out outcomes
questions.explanation: Individual effects are never observed, but group effects on held-out randomised data are, so groups formed by the prediction can be checked.
misconceptions: Uses outcomes, which are not effects, and seekers the model has seen
Checks agreement with another model, not with effects
Measures outcome prediction, not effect prediction

questions.prompt: On held-out seekers, estimator A has a best-linear-predictor slope of 0.9 (se 0.2) and estimator B a slope of 0.1 (se 0.2). Both have the same mean prediction. Which conclusion holds?
options: A's predictions carry real signal about differences in effect; B's carry almost none
B is better calibrated because its slope is closer to zero
Both are equally useful because their averages agree
A overstates differences by 10%
questions.explanation: The slope measures how much observed differences follow predicted ones: near 1 is calibrated, near 0 is no signal.
misconceptions: Thinks the target slope is zero
Judges an effect model by its average, which says nothing about targeting
Reads a slope below 1, within one standard error, as a precise overstatement

questions.prompt: Why do the Qini curves of every ranking end at the same point?
options: Because every ranking was trained on the same data
Because at 100% every ranking coaches everyone, so the extra employed equal the whole effect
Because the curves are normalised to end at 1
Because random allocation is the best any ranking can do at full budget
questions.explanation: At full budget the ranking no longer matters: everyone is coached.
misconceptions: Confuses training data with the end point of the curve
Assumes a normalisation the Qini curve does not use
Reads the shared end point as a limit on rankings

questions.prompt: Switching from ranking by risk to ranking by estimated benefit would move 84% of the places to different seekers and raise the jobs found. What is the data scientist's responsibility here?
options: Recommend the switch: more jobs settle the question
Recommend keeping the risk score, because changing who gets support is unfair
Show who gains and who loses a place, with the jobs at stake, and leave the choice of priority to the decision owner with an audit
Average the two rankings to split the difference
questions.explanation: Who should be prioritised is a value choice; the analysis makes the trade-off visible and audited.
misconceptions: Treats a value choice about who receives support as a technical result
Decides the value question in the other direction without showing the trade-off
Mixes two rules without measuring what the mixture buys or costs

questions.prompt: An agency hands you 30,000 logged decisions with the probability its tool recorded for each. Before valuing any rule, what do you check first?
options: That the outcome model fitted on the logs has a high AUC
That offered divided by recorded probability averages to about 1, overall and by office
That the recorded probabilities lie between 0.05 and 0.95
That the offer rate equals the target budget
questions.explanation: With correct probabilities the weights average to 1; a group where they do not is a group whose records misdescribe the decisions.
misconceptions: Checks the outcome model, which the recorded probabilities do not depend on
Checks a range, which says nothing about whether they describe what happened
Compares with a plan rather than with the records

questions.prompt: One office overrode the allocation tool for a year while the tool kept recording its own probabilities. A candidate rule targets seekers in that office's region. What do you do?
options: Use the recorded probabilities: they are the official record
Drop the office and value the rule on the other offices only, without comment
Re-estimate that office's propensities from its covariates and say so in the report
Clip the office's weights at 20
questions.explanation: When the office matters to the rule, its propensities must be modelled as on Day 1, and the report must say the records were replaced.
misconceptions: Trusts a record the check has shown to be wrong
Drops the region the rule targets and hides the change of population
Treats wrong probabilities as a variance problem

questions.prompt: In inverse propensity valuation of a rule, a seeker whom the logs did not coach but the rule would coach contributes what?
options: Her outcome, weighted by one over the probability of coaching
Nothing: the logs did not do what the rule would do
Her outcome plus the average effect of coaching
Her outcome with weight one
questions.explanation: Only decisions where the logs agree with the rule show the outcome the rule would produce; the weights let them stand in for the rest.
misconceptions: Uses an outcome observed without coaching as if it were under coaching
Imputes an effect the plain IPW estimator never imputes
Forgets that disagreeing decisions are dropped

questions.prompt: You value three rules with inverse propensity weighting and with the augmented estimator. The augmented intervals are all narrower. Why?
options: The augmented estimator uses more data
The outcome model explains part of the outcome, so the weighted residuals vary less than the weighted outcomes
The augmented estimator clips the weights
The augmented estimator assumes no confounding and IPW does not
questions.explanation: Weighting residuals rather than raw outcomes shrinks the variance, while the correction keeps the estimate consistent.
misconceptions: Both use the same decisions
Confuses augmentation with clipping
Both rely on the same identification; the difference is variance

questions.prompt: Two rules have the same estimated value, within 0.1 points: a caseworker rule on months unemployed and a top fifth ranked by a causal forest. Which choice is best defended?
options: The forest: a model that uses more information must be better
Either, chosen by coin toss, since they are equal
The rule caseworkers can read, unless a paired interval shows the other is clearly better
Neither, until a larger dataset separates them
questions.explanation: When the values tie, transparency, auditability and ease of use decide; a paired interval for the difference checks the tie.
misconceptions: Ignores that the table shows no difference in value
Ignores what else separates them
Delays a decision that the table already supports

questions.prompt: A rule would coach 3,000 seekers. The logs coached 130 of them, and their weights have an effective sample size of 60. What does this mean for the value estimate?
options: It rests on the equivalent of about 60 decisions, so it can move a lot with a few of them
It is fine, because 130 coached seekers is above the usual minimum of 30
It is biased downwards by a factor of 60 over 3,000
It is fine if the logs hold 40,000 decisions in total
questions.explanation: Kish's effective sample size tells how many equally weighted decisions carry the estimate; 60 cannot speak reliably for 3,000.
misconceptions: Counts decisions without regard to how unequal their weights are
Treats the effective sample size as a bias correction
Looks at the whole file, not at the seekers the rule changes

questions.prompt: Clipping the weights at 20 moves a rule's value from 55.9% to 54.8%; the next best rule differs by 0.8 points. What do you report?
options: The clipped value, since clipping reduces variance
The unclipped value, since clipping adds bias
The average of the two
That the logs cannot rank this rule, with both values and the effective sample size
questions.explanation: When the sensitivity to a few weights exceeds the gap between rules, the honest report is that the data cannot decide.
misconceptions: Treats a biased fix as the estimate
Hides a sensitivity that is larger than the decision margin
Invents an estimator with no justification

questions.prompt: An analyst reports that seekers who attended four or more coaching sessions gained 27 points. Which flaw matters most?
options: The subgroup is too small
The subgroup is defined by something that happened after the lottery, so it is selected, not randomised
The p-value should be corrected for multiple tests
The analyst should have used a causal forest
questions.explanation: Attendance exists only for coached seekers and depends on traits like motivation; the comparison mixes coaching with selection.
misconceptions: Over 1,500 seekers: size is not the problem
One pre-chosen comparison; the flaw is in its design
A different estimator cannot fix a subgroup defined after treatment

questions.prompt: A memo picks the largest of 60 subgroup effects, 49.5 points in 36 seekers, estimated on the same data used to search. What is your best estimate of its true effect without new data?
options: 49.5 points, since the p-value is 0.001
Much smaller: the winner of a search is inflated by the noise that made it win
Zero, because dredged findings are always false
Exactly the average effect, since all cells are equal
questions.explanation: Selection inflates the largest estimate; honest searches show winners shrinking by about half on fresh seekers.
misconceptions: Ignores that the cell was chosen for being large
Overcorrects: the cell may still benefit
Assumes no real heterogeneity

questions.prompt: Of 60 cells, 52 have p above 0.05. The memo says coaching "showed no effect" in them. What is wrong?
options: Nothing: p above 0.05 means no effect
Cells of 30 to 60 seekers have too little power to show a real effect of about 10 points
The threshold should have been 0.10
Those cells should be merged into one and tested again
questions.explanation: A non-significant small cell is uninformative; its interval includes both no effect and the average effect.
misconceptions: Reads absence of significance as evidence of absence
Moves the threshold instead of reading the uncertainty
A remedy, not a diagnosis of what the memo got wrong
